transcript: A starry Rocky Horror revival has landed on Broadway. And while there are a lot of really great elements, I do ultimately feel like one major misstep really brings down the entire production. But before I get to that, I do wanna talk about the things I think this production does really well, starting with the direction by Sam Pinkleton, which I think is appropriately campy and creepy and sexy. The movie has become so iconic that I think there is often this impulse to just copy whatever the movie did. I think they did a really good job at avoiding that impulse and instead providing a really new take on this show and these characters while still feeling true to the spirit of the original. This is true of the performances as well. The standouts for me being Luke Evans as Frank-N-furter, Stephanie Hsu as Janet and Amber Gray as Riff Raff. And the entire theatre has been completely decked out to match the tone of this production. There are skeletons and grey mannequins, there's tubing along the wall and the first rows of seats have been covered in tin foil. You immediately feel transported into the strange and off beat world. As I alluded to before, I think the one thing this production really hasn't quite figured out is the callbacks, which have become a major part of the Rocky Horror experience thanks to rowdy, interactive screenings of the film version that have been going on for decades. Now, this production has actually changed their guidance on callbacks a couple of times over the course of the preview process, but it basically landed on don't be an asshole, which is a sentiment I definitely agree with, but is ultimately vague and subjective. And, at least at my performance, LED to an audience that was afraid to shout anything out. We did have a few moments of callbacks where someone would shout something out and the actors would respond. And I wanted more of that, because that is part of the fun of doing call outs with live actors is, unlike a movie, they can actually hear you and respond to you. But those moments were few and far between, at least at my performance. And I think the overall production was worse off for it. And I do wonder if this show would have been better off providing a list of pre approved call outs or even projecting call outs at the top of the stage so that everyone can participate. Because Rocky Horror at its best should feel like a communal experience where everyone feels like they are a part of it. And when you only have literally three people in the audience doing call outs, it just doesn't have the same impact.
classificationReason: First-hand Broadway review at Studio 54 with clear opinions on Sam Pinkleton's direction, standout performances (Luke Evans, Stephanie Hsu, Amber Gray), and the immersive theater design.
